transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came in because at church I’ve been doing some odd things. Like I’ll stand by the potluck table holding the serving spoon up and just not move, or I’ll keep folding the same stack of napkins over and over while people are waiting on me. It’s embarrassing, and I don’t really know why I’m doing it.
Do you feel anxious or distressed while you're doing these things, or do they seem to happen without any particular emotion attached?

It doesn’t feel like I’m upset right then, really. It just sort of happens. I’ll be standing there with the serving spoon up, not moving, or folding those napkins again and again, and people are waiting. Then afterward I feel embarrassed because I know it looked odd.

When you find yourself holding the serving spoon without moving or folding the napkins repeatedly, do you have any particular thoughts going through your mind, or does it feel like you have to do it a certain way?

I don’t really have a thought like, “I have to do it this exact way.” It’s more like I just get stuck doing it. I’ll be there at the potluck holding the spoon up, or I’ll keep folding the same napkins even though folks are waiting, and I don’t quite know why I’m doing it.
When you’re holding the spoon up or folding the napkins repeatedly, do you realize at that moment that what you’re doing might not make sense, or does it feel more automatic without much thought?

At the moment, it feels more automatic, like I’m just stuck there doing it. I don’t really stop and think, “This doesn’t make sense,” until after, when I see people waiting or looking at me. Then I feel embarrassed about it.
While you're holding the spoon up or folding the napkins, is there any part of you that notices or thinks, 'I should stop this,' or does it feel like you're not even aware of it until it's over?

I don’t think I really notice it right then. It’s like I’m just there by the potluck table, holding the spoon up, or messing with the same napkins, and I’m not thinking, “Stop now.” I usually realize more when people are waiting on me or looking at me.
While you're holding the spoon or folding the napkins, is there any part of you that wants to stop but feels like you can't, or does it feel more like you're not even aware of what you're doing?

It feels more like I’m not aware of what I’m doing right then. I’m just standing there at church with the serving spoon held up, or I’m folding those napkins again and again, and people are waiting. I don’t feel like I’m fighting to stop—it’s more like I’ve gotten stuck somehow.
While you're doing these things—like holding the spoon up or folding the napkins—do you have any awareness at all that you're doing them, or does it feel like you're on autopilot the whole time?

It feels like I’m on autopilot most of the time. I’ll be at church by the potluck table, just holding that serving spoon up and not moving, or folding the same napkins over and over, and I don’t really catch myself until people are waiting or staring.
Before you start holding the spoon up or folding the napkins, do you ever feel a sudden urge or need to do it, like something is pulling you to start the action?

I don’t really feel a sudden urge before it starts. It’s more like I’m just there at church and then I realize I’m doing something odd, like holding the serving spoon up and not moving, or folding that same stack of napkins again while people are waiting on me.

Before you start doing these repetitive things at church, like holding the spoon up or folding the napkins, do you ever feel any kind of physical sensation, urge, or change in your body or mind that comes right before it starts?

No, I don’t notice any feeling right before it. I don’t feel something in my body telling me to do it. I’ll just be at church, and then I’m standing there with the spoon up and not moving, or I’m folding those napkins again while people are waiting. It just sort of happens.
While you're holding the spoon up or folding the napkins repeatedly, do you feel fully aware of what's going on around you, or does it feel like you're spaced out or not fully present?

I think I’m kind of spaced out when it happens. Like at the church potluck, I’ll be standing there holding the serving spoon up, not moving, or folding the same napkins again and again, and I don’t really feel fully present until I notice people are waiting on me.
While you're holding the spoon up or folding the napkins, do you know where you are, like recognizing you're at church or who is around you?
I’m not really sure. I think I know I’m at church, but when I’m doing it, I’m not paying much attention to who’s around me. It’s more like I come back to it when I notice people are waiting.
While you're holding the spoon up or folding the napkins, do you ever feel confused about where you are, what you're doing, or lose track of who you are?

I don’t think I lose track of who I am. It’s more that I’m just doing those odd things at church—like holding the serving spoon up and not moving, or folding the same napkins over and over—and people are waiting on me. Then I sort of notice it.
After you finish holding the spoon up or folding the napkins repeatedly, can you remember what happened during that time, or does it feel like there’s a gap in your memory of what occurred?

I’m not real sure. I can usually remember that I was there and that people were waiting, but the middle of it is kind of fuzzy. I don’t know if I’d call it a full gap, just… I don’t remember every bit of what I was thinking or doing right then.

latest_inference.note: The patient's description of being on autopilot, not aware of the behavior during the episodes, and having a fuzzy memory of the events as they happen, supports an organic or neurological cause rather than a primary psychiatric condition like OCD or anxiety. The lack of intrusive thoughts, urges, or distress further rules out F42.2 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder).
